report.source_text: On physical exam, the patient was in mild distress. Vital signs showed blood pressure at 106/48, heart rate 86 bpm, afebrile at 36.8 C, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Patient had regular heart rate and rhythm; no murmurs were auscultated; lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally, no rales, wheezing or rhonchi were heard; abdominal examination was positive for generalized abdominal tenderness, without any palpable masses, guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness. The ostomy was patent, pink with an ileostomy bag filled with fluid and gas.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Paroxysmal arial fibrillation was determined to be the culprit of her splenic infarct
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 68-year-old female with colonic Crohn’s disease underwent colectomy with ileostomy and presented with persistent nausea, abdominal pain, high ostomy output, and weakness. Initial physical exam showed regular heart rhythm. Abdominal contrast CT confirmed multiple splenic infarcts with branch splenic artery occlusion. Telemetry monitoring during hospitalization detected an episode of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation that reverted to sinus rhythm. Negative phospholipid antibody and JAK2 mutation testing ruled out other hypercoagulable causes. The patient was diagnosed with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation as the source of embolic splenic infarct and discharged on anticoagulation (apixaban) and rate control (metoprolol).
